html:
How this works

TX-NOMINATE places every member of the Texas House and Senate since statehood on a map using nothing but their record votes. Members who vote alike end up close together, and members who usually vote against each other end up far apart. It's a Texas version of DW-NOMINATE, the method behind Voteview's maps of Congress.

200,065record votes, 1st–89th Legislatures (1846–2025)
99,781contested votes used to draw the map
5,319legislators placed
6,924,220individual yea and nay votes

Reading the map

  • Every legislature from 1846 to 2025 is on one map. A member keeps a single position for their whole career, and careers overlap, so each legislature is tied to the ones before and after it by the members they share. A score of +0.4 means the same place in 1925 as in 2025.
  • The place is fixed, but what it stands for isn't. Left to right is the main line along which Texas votes split, and up and down is the second. Who sits where changes as the issues and parties change. Below the map on each page is a short guide to what the axes meant in those years; the full list is below.
  • Scores run from −1 to +1 and only describe positions relative to other Texas legislators. A "moderate" here is someone between the blocs in Austin, not a moderate by any national standard.
  • Only contested votes count. A vote counts as contested when at least 2.5% of those voting were on the losing side. Most record votes are near-unanimous and say nothing about who disagrees with whom. They're still listed in the vote explorer.
  • On a vote's page, the dashed line is the cutting line. It's where the model draws the split for that vote: members on the shaded side are expected to vote yea, members on the other side nay. Members on the "wrong" side are the surprises.

What the axes mean, era by era

The labels come from looking at who sits at each end in each era, which roll calls split along each axis, and where the members' home counties are. They describe tendencies, not verdicts on any member.

1846–1873: statehood, Civil War and Reconstruction

Left to right: the main divide. Before the Civil War there was no lasting two-party divide in Austin, and the axis is hard to name: the fire-eater Louis T. Wigfall sits well to the left and the Unionist James W. Throckmorton near the center, but with so few members' parties on record, two careers can't say what the sides stood for. In the Reconstruction House of 1870–73, Republicans sit mostly to the left and Democrats to the right. Most members before Reconstruction have no party on record.

Up and down: no strong pattern. Only a weak pattern: Houston and the border counties (Starr, Webb) sit somewhat low, and rural East and North Texas slightly high. Most votes split left to right, so read the map mainly that way.

1874–1900: after Reconstruction

Left to right: reform to conservative. Democrats held most seats, and the main divide ran through them. On regulating corporations and trusts and on protecting labor unions, reformers sit to the left and their opponents to the right. The parties that challenged the Democrats land on different sides by decade: Republicans and Greenbackers of the 1870s and 1880s sit to the left, while the Populists of the 1890s and the Republicans who worked with them sit to the right. In this era the axis partly tracks who opposed the Democratic majority at the time, not one fixed ideology.

Up and down: countryside to cities and border. Members from the rural Anglo counties, especially in North Texas, sit at the top. At the bottom are the cities (Galveston, Houston, San Antonio, Beaumont), the border counties such as Webb, and the German counties (Fayette, DeWitt, Blanco). Most votes still split left to right, but about a third split up and down.

1901–1930: prohibition and the Progressive Era

Left to right: progressive to conservative. Progressives sit to the left, conservatives to the right. Prohibition, the era's defining fight, runs mostly up and down the map instead: on the 1911 and 1913 liquor votes the drys sit at the top and the wets at the bottom, with the drys a little to the left.

Up and down: dry countryside to wet cities. The top is the dry countryside: rural Anglo counties of East, North and West Texas. The bottom is the wet Texas of San Antonio, Houston, Galveston and Beaumont, the border, and the German and Czech counties of Central Texas. With nearly every member a Democrat, this regional and cultural split decided about as many votes as the left–right one.

1931–1960: New Deal liberals and conservative Democrats

Left to right: liberal to conservative. Liberal Democrats such as Maury Maverick Jr. and Henry B. González sit to the left, and conservative Democrats such as Dorsey Hardeman, Wardlow Lane and Coke Stevenson to the right.

Up and down: countryside to cities and border. As before 1930, rural Anglo counties of East and North Texas sit at the top, and the big cities (Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth, San Antonio) and the Rio Grande Valley at the bottom. In these one-party decades this was still the most common way votes split.

1961–1982: liberals, conservatives and the first Republicans

Left to right: liberal to conservative. Liberals such as Bob Eckhardt, Barbara Jordan, Oscar Mauzy and Sissy Farenthold sit to the left, conservative Democrats to the right. The first modern Republicans join the conservatives on the right.

Up and down: countryside to cities. Rural and small-city members sit at the top, and the Dallas delegation at the bottom, with Fort Worth, El Paso, Laredo and Duval County also below the middle. Most contested votes now cut across both axes at once.

1983–1994: the Republicans' rise

Left to right: liberal to conservative. Liberal Democrats to the left, Republicans to the right, with conservative rural Democrats in between.

Up and down: Republican suburbs to Democratic Texas. As Republicans won the suburbs, this axis came to separate them (top: Collin, Denton and Midland counties, suburban Dallas) from Democrats, rural and urban alike (bottom). Party now shows up on both axes.

1995–2025: the two-party era

Left to right: liberal to conservative. Almost entirely Democrats against Republicans. In the 1990s, when many rural and South Texas Democrats voted conservatively, the parties overlapped much more.

Up and down: establishment to anti-establishment. Within both parties, this separates members who vote with their chamber's leadership from those who buck it. Among House Republicans, the top is each era's Speaker's team: Talmadge Heflin and Fred Hill under Craddick, Stan Lambert more recently. The bottom is the rebels: Jonathan Stickland, Brian Harrison and Andy Hopper. Among Democrats, mavericks like Terry Canales sit lowest. In the Senate the axis separates institutionalists such as Robert Nichols and Charles Schwertner from members such as Mayes Middleton and Sarah Eckhardt.

How many dimensions?

The model can use as many axes as you like, but each additional one has to earn its place. Here's how well the map predicts members' yea and nay votes with one, two and three dimensions:

DimensionsVotes predicted correctlyAPRE
181.3%0.27
284.7%0.40
386.0%0.45

APRE (aggregate proportional reduction in error) is the share of the losing-side votes the model gets right beyond the trivial guess that everyone voted with the majority. 0 means no better than that guess and 1 means perfect.

The second dimension earns its place: it cuts the remaining errors by about a fifth. A third adds much less, and it has no clear, stable meaning across eras, so the maps show the first two.

One map for 180 years?

Texas politics changed completely between 1846 and today, so we tested whether one shared map really fits every era. For each era we fitted a separate map using only that era's votes, hid one vote in ten from both the shared map and the era's own map, and asked each to predict the hidden votes. With a good starting point, the shared map predicts the hidden votes about as well as the era-only maps, or better, in every era from the antebellum legislatures to today. So we use one map and accept that its axes mean different things in different eras, as Voteview does for Congress.

Where the votes come from

  • 1846 to the 1990s: the Legislative Reference Library's scanned journals. The Library has scanned every House and Senate Journal since statehood. We read the vote lists from the scans' text, and re-read pages with Tesseract OCR where that text is too garbled. Old journals print a vote as running lists of surnames ("Yeas—Messrs. Allen, Baker of Travis …—52"), often split across columns and pages.
  • 1995 on (House) and 1999 on (Senate): the Legislature's own journal website, which publishes clean text. The 1995–97 Senate comes from the Library's copies.
  • Who's who comes from the Library's Texas Legislators: Past & Present: names, parties, districts, counties and exact service dates, plus its lists of Speakers and presidents pro tempore. Early journals rarely record party, so most members before Reconstruction show as "not recorded".
  • The journals name members by surname ("Bell, C.", "Taylor of Collin", "Mr. Speaker"). Each name is matched to one member using that session's roster, initials, counties and service dates, allowing for OCR misreadings. Where the Senate prints only the nays and absentees, the yeas are everyone else serving that day.
  • Every roll call is checked name by name against the totals printed in the journal. A roll call is used only if every name is matched and the counts agree (within one vote where the journal itself miscounts). 18,910 roll calls that couldn't be verified are left out rather than guessed, which is most of the gaps you'll see in the older legislatures. A few journals are missing altogether: the House Journals for 1861–62 and 1864 survive only as newspaper reconstructions with almost no roll calls.
  • The House from 1973 to 1982 isn't here yet. In those years the House Journal printed each vote as a photographed tally sheet, a grid of names and marks, rather than as a list of names. Reading those sheets reliably needs its own reader, which we're still building.

The method

DW-NOMINATE (Poole and Rosenthal) gives each legislator an ideal point and each roll call two outcomes, yea and nay, placed in the same space. A legislator tends to vote for whichever outcome is closer, with some randomness. The positions that best explain every vote at once are the map. Each member keeps one position for their whole career, which is DW-NOMINATE's "constant" model. We tried letting positions drift in a straight line, as Voteview does for Congress, but that let the whole map slowly rotate, so that "left–right" meant something different in one decade than another. Holding positions fixed keeps the map itself stable. The House and Senate share one scale, linked by the 390 members who served in both chambers.

A map this big is easy to get stuck on a poor solution, so the fit starts from the era-by-era maps, joined into one frame through the members who served in neighbouring eras, and then refines everything together.

We wrote our own implementation from the published model, because Voteview's code isn't licensed for reuse. To check it, we ran it on U.S. House votes from the 110th–117th Congresses (2007–2022). In one dimension our scores correlate 0.988 with Voteview's published DW-NOMINATE scores (0.90 or better within each party). Second dimensions are harder to compare. Voteview's comes from one fit of every Congress since 1789, anchored by the era of the Solid South, while a fit of 2007–2022 alone finds that era's own second divide, so the two correlate only 0.40.

Against Shor and McCarty's state legislator scores (1993 on), the standard academic measure, our first dimension correlates 0.91 across 549 Texas legislators: 0.86 among Democrats and 0.61 among Republicans. Theirs combine roll calls with a national candidate survey, so they won't match exactly.

Caveats

  • Record votes aren't the whole story. Much of the Legislature's work happens in committee and in what never comes to a vote. Before the 1970s, many votes were taken by voice and never recorded name by name.
  • Older legislatures have fewer verified votes, because the scans are harder to read. A member with few contested votes has a less certain position.
  • The Speaker rarely votes, so a Speaker's position comes mostly from their votes before taking the gavel.
  • Members with fewer than 20 contested votes aren't placed on the map, though their votes still appear in the explorer.
  • "Liberal" and "conservative" are labels for the axis, not verdicts on any member. In some eras the axis tracks something else, such as who was in the majority and who opposed it; the era guide says where.

Data and code

Download the data: members.csv, member_scores.csv (positions by legislature), rollcalls.csv.gz, votes.csv.gz. The code that builds everything, from downloading the journals to fitting the model, is on GitHub.

Built 2026-10-27. Scores are re-estimated as more votes are added, so they can shift a little between versions.
